screens.title: Scripted Package Installation
screens.narratorSegment: Automating package installation means your script runs the package manager in a non-interactive mode and verifies results. A practical pattern is to refresh package lists, then install with an automatic yes flag so prompts never block the script. For example, a provisioning script on a Debian-based host will run the update command followed by an install command with the yes flag to avoid confirmations. The important follow-up is checking the command's exit status: if the install failed, the script should either retry, log the failure, or abort further configuration steps so you don't proceed with a broken setup. Common mistakes include forgetting to elevate privileges or omitting the yes flag, which causes scripts to pause waiting for input. Another pitfall is assuming network access is available; good scripts check network reachability before attempting package operations. As a concrete example, imagine bootstrapping a web server: you refresh package lists, install the web server package non-interactively, and then test that the package command returned success before enabling and starting the service. A final tip: keep package manager commands idempotent by checking for the package first or relying on install commands that are safe to run multiple times, so your script behaves predictably when re-run. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Scripted Package Installation
Concept
Refresh package lists, install with an auto-confirm flag, and always verify exit status before continuing.
Why the yes flag matters
Prevents interactive prompts from stopping automation, which is essential in provisioning scripts.
Common mistake
Forgetting to run with elevated privileges causes permission errors and failed installs.
Key Takeaway

Always use non-interactive flags for automation and check exit codes to avoid hidden failures.

Code example (provisioning pattern)
#!/bin/bash
set -e
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nginx
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Package install failed" >&2
  exit 1
fi
# Continue with configuration only if the install succeeded
sudo systemctl enable nginx
sudo systemctl start nginx
Concrete example
A provisioning script installs nginx without prompts, exits on failure, then enables the service for boot.
Check your understanding
Name one additional check you would add before starting the service. (Answer: verify package is installed or test listening port.)

screens.title: Automation Flags & Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Flags and permissions are small details that determine whether automation succeeds or silently stalls. The automatic confirmation flag in package managers tells the tool to accept prompts; without it the package manager will wait for user input and your script will pause. Running commands with elevated privileges is necessary because package installation and service management modify system state. If you forget to use elevation, package commands fail with permission errors. Beyond flags and permissions, robust automation checks the exit status produced by each command. This status reports whether the action succeeded and lets the script decide to continue, retry, or halt. A common misconception is to assume that a displayed package manager summary implies success; instead, always use the literal exit status or specific checks like testing that a package binary exists. For example, after an install you can query whether the service binary is present or call the package manager's status query. In short, automation needs both non-interactive options and defensive checks to be safe when re-run, especially on new or flaky networks. What defensive check will you add to your next script to catch failed installs early?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Automation Flags & Error Handling
Concept cards
Non-interactive flags
The yes flag prevents prompts. Always include it in unattended scripts.
Privilege elevation
Use sudo or run scripts as root if needed; permission errors will otherwise abort the flow.
Exit status checks
Check the return code or test for expected files before proceeding to dependent steps.
Quick code patterns
# check exit code pattern
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y htop
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Install failed, aborting" >&2
  exit 1
fi
# alternative: check for binary
if command -v htop > /dev/null; then
  echo "htop installed"
fi
Concrete example
After installing Nginx, test that the Nginx binary exists before you try to enable the service.
Common mistake
Assuming success because the package manager printed progress; always check the command's exit code.

screens.title: Updating and Upgrading Packages in Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Updating packages in automation has a small but important sequence: refresh package lists, apply upgrades if needed, and verify outcomes. On Debian-family systems you refresh the lists first so install commands use current metadata. For upgrades you run the upgrade operation non-interactively; this ensures security updates are applied without intervention. In scripts, combine commands so later steps don't run if the prior step failed. For example, chaining update and upgrade with logical AND ensures the upgrade only runs on a successful update. Be careful with full upgrades in unattended environments: major package changes can require manual conflict resolution or service restarts that you must plan for. A safer approach for automation is to limit upgrades to security patches or schedule full upgrades during maintenance windows. As an example, automating a daily security update can be scripted to update lists, apply upgrades, log the output, and email or report failures. The misconception to avoid is treating automated upgrades as invisible; always capture logs, handle non-zero exit codes, and test upgrades on staging before applying to production. What logging or rollback step would you add to your upgrade automation?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Updating & Upgrading
Recommended process
Step 1: Refresh lists
Ensure package metadata is current before installs or upgrades.
Step 2: Apply upgrades carefully
Use non-interactive flags; consider limiting to security updates for unattended runs.
Step 3: Log and verify
Capture output and check exit codes so you can detect and respond to problems.
Script snippet and example
# safe upgrade pattern
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y >& upgrade.log
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Upgrade failed, see upgrade.log" >&2
  # optional: alert or rollback steps
fi
Concrete scenario
Schedule a nightly security-only upgrade job, log output, and only escalate on non-zero exit codes to on-call.
Misconception
Assuming all upgrades are safe unattended; large upgrades can need manual conflict resolution.

screens.title: Managing Services with systemctl
screens.narratorSegment: Managing services is the next step after installing software. The systemctl command is the primary interface to systemd for controlling these services. You use it to start or stop a service immediately, to restart it after configuration changes, and to enable it so it starts on boot. Typical script commands include start, stop, restart, enable, disable, and status queries. A common pattern is to enable at the end of a setup to ensure services come up after a reboot and to start immediately so the service is available right away. When scripting, it is useful to check whether a service is already active before restarting it to avoid confusing logs or unintended restarts. For example, many scripts check active state and then restart only if necessary. The misconception to correct is that enabling a service starts it immediately; enabling schedules it for boot and you still need to run start for immediate effect. In automation, combine service commands with exit checks and clear logging so you can audit what your script changed. Managing Services with systemctl means use systemctl to control the runtime state and boot behavior of services; enable schedules boot start, start runs now.. In practical terms, start, stop, restart, enable, and check service status programmatically. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Managing Services
Common systemctl commands
Start / Stop
Start runs the service now; stop halts it immediately.
Enable / Disable
Enable ensures the service starts on boot; it does not necessarily start the service immediately.
Status checks
Use is-active for scripts and status for detailed logs useful when debugging.
Example patterns
# enable for boot, then start now
sudo systemctl enable nginx
sudo systemctl start nginx

# conditional restart
if systemctl is-active nginx; then
  sudo systemctl restart nginx
fi
Concrete example
Enable a firewall service to ensure it is present after reboot, and start it to enforce rules immediately.
Misconception
Enabling alone does not start a service in the current session; plan for both enable and start when provisioning.

screens.title: Conditional Service Management in Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: When automating service changes, you don't always want to restart unconditionally. Restarting a service that is already down may be a no-op or it may mask a deeper failure. Many administrators prefer to check whether a service is active before restarting it, or to start it only when it's inactive. The systemctl is-active command returns a simple success code for active state, which scripts can use in conditional statements. This pattern prevents unnecessary restarts and provides clearer logging. For instance, a script can test is-active and only call restart if the service is active, otherwise it can start it. Another useful pattern is to capture the detailed status output when a service is not active to aid debugging. A common misconception is that a restart always recovers a failing service; sometimes debugging or configuration changes are required first. In an automation workflow, prefer conditional logic that records what was done, and include a path for alerting or halting further steps if a service fails to reach the expected state. How would you log a failed start so an operator can quickly diagnose the issue?

keyIdea.title: Check before you restart
keyIdea.text: Use systemctl is-active in scripts to decide whether to restart, start, or report the service state to operators.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Conditional Service Management
Patterns for safe service updates
Active check
Use a simple active check to decide the correct operation and avoid noisy restarts.
Record decisions
Log whether you started, restarted, or failed so operators can trace automation actions.
Fallbacks
If a start fails, capture status output and stop further configuration until an operator investigates.
Conditional code example
# conditional restart example
if systemctl is-active nginx; then
  sudo systemctl restart nginx
  echo "nginx restarted" >> /var/log/automation.log
else
  sudo systemctl start nginx || { systemctl status nginx && echo "start failed, see status" >&2; exit 1; }
fi
Concrete example
Only restart a web server if it was running, otherwise start it and capture status to aid debugging.
Check your understanding
Why might a restart not resolve an outage? (Answer: configuration errors or missing dependencies require fixes, not restarts.)

screens.title: What is a systemd Unit File?
screens.narratorSegment: A systemd unit file is a plain text configuration that tells systemd how to manage a resource. The most common type for automation is the service unit, which has at least three sections: Unit, Service, and Install. The Unit section describes metadata such as a human-readable description and dependencies like network availability. The Service section defines how to run the process, for example the command to start the script and restart policy. The Install section states how the unit is attached to boot targets. A concrete example in the chapter shows a simple unit that runs a script, restarts on failure, and binds to the multi-user boot target. After editing or creating a unit file you must reload systemd's configuration so it recognizes the change. A common misconception is that unit files are binary or specialized files; they are editable text and can be managed like other configuration files. Knowing the key fields lets you craft reliable service behavior: choose an appropriate restart policy, set After dependencies to delay start until required resources are present, and ensure WantedBy points to a sensible target for enabling.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › systemd Unit File
Unit file anatomy
[Unit]
Metadata and dependencies, for example Description and After.
[Service]
ExecStart, Restart policy, and Type controls how the process is launched and kept alive.
[Install]
Defines how the unit is enabled, often WantedBy=multi-user.target for typical services.
Example unit file
[Unit]
Description=My Custom Automation Script
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/my_automation_script.sh
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Concrete example
This unit runs a script after the network is available and restarts on failure, then is enabled for the multi-user target.
Action reminder
After saving a unit file run daemon-reload, enable, and start to apply it.

screens.title: Deploying a Custom systemd Unit
screens.narratorSegment: Turning a script into a managed service follows a clear deployment sequence. First, author the unit file in the system directory and confirm the ExecStart path points to an executable script. Next, reload systemd's configuration so it discovers your new unit. Without reloading, systemd will not know about the file. Then enable the unit to create the boot-time symlink so the service will be started on reboot. Finally, start the service for immediate effect. In practice you will run these three commands after creating the file: reload the daemon, enable the unit, then start it. Each step is idempotent in the sense that re-running enable or start is generally safe; daemon-reload should be run whenever unit files change. A common mistake is to forget to make the script executable, which causes start to fail; another is forgetting the After dependencies, which can result in the service starting before required resources are ready. As a concrete lab, you will create a hello-world script that appends a timestamp to a log file, make it executable, author a unit file, reload the daemon, enable, and start the service, then verify the log file contains the message. What check will you perform after starting the unit to confirm it works?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › setup_webserver.sh Walkthrough
Script structure
Start safely
Use a shell header and options to exit on error so subsequent steps don't run on partial failures.
Install and check
Run update and install with non-interactive flags and test the exit code before changing services.
Enable & start
Enable makes the service start at boot; start makes it run now for immediate availability.
Example script excerpt
# setup_webserver.sh
#!/bin/bash
set -e
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nginx
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Nginx install failed" >&2
  exit 1
fi
sudo systemctl enable nginx
sudo systemctl start nginx
systemctl is-active --quiet nginx && echo "Nginx is running." || echo "Nginx is NOT running."

After running, check the service status and open the default web page to confirm the server responds.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Hello-world Service
hello_world.sh
#!/bin/bash
echo "Hello from my custom systemd service at $(date)!" >> /tmp/hello_log.txt
Make it executable
Run chmod +x on the script so systemd can execute it via ExecStart.
Unit file & verification
[Unit]
Description=My Hello World Script
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/hello_world.sh
Type=simple
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Verify
Run daemon-reload, enable, start, then check /tmp/hello_log.txt for appended messages.
Troubleshooting
If no log appears, check ExecStart path, script permissions, and systemctl status for errors.

screens.title: Scripts vs Configuration Management Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Shell scripts are great for single-server automation and quick bootstrapping tasks because they run locally and you control every command. But when managing many servers, repeating scripts manually becomes error-prone and hard to maintain. Configuration management tools like Ansible are agentless and operate over SSH, letting you declare desired state or run ad-hoc modules across groups of hosts defined in an inventory. One advantage of Ansible is idempotence: tasks are designed so reapplying them yields the same result rather than creating duplicates or unintended changes. Use scripts when you need a simple, fast, one-off setup and use configuration management when you need consistency across multiple hosts and the ability to reapply changes safely. A concrete Ansible example is running an ad-hoc module to install nginx across a group of web servers listed in an inventory file. A common misconception is that Ansible replaces shell entirely; in practice, Ansible often calls shell commands or uses modules that wrap package managers and service control for you. Start with ad-hoc commands to prove connectivity and then move to playbooks for repeatable runs. Which approach fits your environment today: a focused script or a small Ansible inventory?

In this chapter we focus on making system administration repeatable. You will learn how to put package manager commands into scripts so installs and upgrades run unattended, how to manage long-running programs with systemd and systemctl, and when to reach for a configuration management tool like Ansible to scale tasks across many servers. Automation removes human repetition and reduces drift, but it also requires attention to error handling, correct flags, and service lifecycle. I'll show concrete, safe examples that work on Debian-family systems and note the equivalent package actions for RHEL-family distributions. You will also see how a custom systemd unit file turns a script into a managed service that restarts on failure and can be enabled at boot. Finally, you'll get a short introduction to Ansible's inventory and ad-hoc commands so you understand how a single command can install a package across many hosts. As you go through the lesson, think about one task you repeat on new servers today and imagine automating it: what would change, and what checks would you need to add?

These learning objectives make the chapter practical and testable. First, you'll automate package installation, updates, and removal inside shell scripts so provisioning runs unattended and repeatable. That skill matters because packages are the base of any service you deploy and unattended installs prevent manual mistakes during scale-ups. Second, you'll manage system services with the systemctl command so services can be started, stopped, enabled at boot, and queried programmatically. Knowing the service lifecycle avoids outages when deploying changes. Third, you'll understand systemd unit file structure so you can wrap custom scripts as managed services with restart behavior and dependency ordering. A correct unit file lets systemd supervise your automation reliably. Finally, you'll perform basic ad-hoc commands with a configuration management tool such as Ansible, which demonstrates how one command can affect many hosts consistently. This matters because manual repetition across many servers is error-prone; ad-hoc management shows the first step toward full infrastructure as code. Each objective pairs practice with a short verification step so you can confirm competency.

This second objectives slide focuses on verification, error handling, and a hands-on lab. You will learn to check exit statuses after package commands so your script can abort or retry when an install fails. That prevents cascading failures during provisioning. Next, you'll learn the sequence of daemon-reload, enable, and start after authoring a unit file so systemd recognizes and runs your new service. Practically, you'll create a hello world script that writes to a log file and then confirm the log contains the expected message. You will also learn to craft an inventory file for Ansible and run ad-hoc commands to ping hosts and ensure a package is present. Finally, the lab ties these pieces together: a script that installs Nginx, enables and starts it, and a custom unit for a simple logging script. Each objective maps to a short verification step so you can confirm competency in a real environment.

Automating package installation means your script runs the package manager in a non-interactive mode and verifies results. A practical pattern is to refresh package lists, then install with an automatic yes flag so prompts never block the script. For example, a provisioning script on a Debian-based host will run the update command followed by an install command with the yes flag to avoid confirmations. The important follow-up is checking the command's exit status: if the install failed, the script should either retry, log the failure, or abort further configuration steps so you don't proceed with a broken setup. Common mistakes include forgetting to elevate privileges or omitting the yes flag, which causes scripts to pause waiting for input. Another pitfall is assuming network access is available; good scripts check network reachability before attempting package operations. As a concrete example, imagine bootstrapping a web server: you refresh package lists, install the web server package non-interactively, and then test that the package command returned success before enabling and starting the service. A final tip: keep package manager commands idempotent by checking for the package first or relying on install commands that are safe to run multiple times, so your script behaves predictably when re-run. Can you describe which check you'd add to ensure an install succeeded before configuring the service?

Flags and permissions are small details that determine whether automation succeeds or silently stalls. The automatic confirmation flag in package managers tells the tool to accept prompts; without it the package manager will wait for user input and your script will pause. Running commands with elevated privileges is necessary because package installation and service management modify system state. If you forget to use elevation, package commands fail with permission errors. Beyond flags and permissions, robust automation checks the exit status produced by each command. This status reports whether the action succeeded and lets the script decide to continue, retry, or halt. A common misconception is to assume that a displayed package manager summary implies success; instead, always use the literal exit status or specific checks like testing that a package binary exists. For example, after an install you can query whether the service binary is present or call the package manager's status query. In short, automation needs both non-interactive options and defensive checks to be safe when re-run, especially on new or flaky networks. What defensive check will you add to your next script to catch failed installs early?

Updating packages in automation has a small but important sequence: refresh package lists, apply upgrades if needed, and verify outcomes. On Debian-family systems you refresh the lists first so install commands use current metadata. For upgrades you run the upgrade operation non-interactively; this ensures security updates are applied without intervention. In scripts, combine commands so later steps don't run if the prior step failed. For example, chaining update and upgrade with logical AND ensures the upgrade only runs on a successful update. Be careful with full upgrades in unattended environments: major package changes can require manual conflict resolution or service restarts that you must plan for. A safer approach for automation is to limit upgrades to security patches or schedule full upgrades during maintenance windows. As an example, automating a daily security update can be scripted to update lists, apply upgrades, log the output, and email or report failures. The misconception to avoid is treating automated upgrades as invisible; always capture logs, handle non-zero exit codes, and test upgrades on staging before applying to production. What logging or rollback step would you add to your upgrade automation?

Managing services is the next step after installing software. The systemctl command is the primary interface to systemd for controlling these services. You use it to start or stop a service immediately, to restart it after configuration changes, and to enable it so it starts on boot. Typical script commands include start, stop, restart, enable, disable, and status queries. A common pattern is to enable at the end of a setup to ensure services come up after a reboot and to start immediately so the service is available right away. For example, many scripts check active state and then restart only if necessary. The misconception to correct is that enabling a service starts it immediately; enabling schedules it for boot and you still need to run start for immediate effect. In automation, combine service commands with exit checks and clear logging so you can audit what your script changed. Managing Services with systemctl means use systemctl to control the runtime state and boot behavior of services; enable schedules boot start, start runs now.. In practical terms, start, stop, restart, enable, and check service status programmatically. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Many administrators prefer to check whether a service is active before restarting it, or to start it only when it's inactive. The systemctl is-active command returns a simple success code for active state, which scripts can use in conditional statements. This pattern prevents unnecessary restarts and provides clearer logging. For instance, a script can test is-active and only call restart if the service is active, otherwise it can start it. Another useful pattern is to capture the detailed status output when a service is not active to aid debugging. A common misconception is that a restart always recovers a failing service; sometimes debugging or configuration changes are required first. In an automation workflow, prefer conditional logic that records what was done, and include a path for alerting or halting further steps if a service fails to reach the expected state. How would you log a failed start so an operator can quickly diagnose the issue?

A systemd unit file is a plain text configuration that tells systemd how to manage a resource. The most common type for automation is the service unit, which has at least three sections: Unit, Service, and Install. The Unit section describes metadata such as a human-readable description and dependencies like network availability. The Service section defines how to run the process, for example the command to start the script and restart policy. The Install section states how the unit is attached to boot targets. After editing or creating a unit file you must reload systemd's configuration so it recognizes the change. Knowing the key fields lets you craft reliable service behavior: choose an appropriate restart policy, set After dependencies to delay start until required resources are present, and ensure WantedBy points to a sensible target for enabling.
